article_excerpt: Opera isn't normally a field associated with animal cruelty, but the two worlds have collided in China after a singer posted pictures of herself wearing a headdress made from kingfisher feathers. Web users and conservationists quickly criticised her indifference towards animal welfare after it emerged the accessory was made from the feathers of no less than 80 of the colourful birds, according to the People's Daily Online. Outcry: Opera singer Liu Guijuan is heavily criticised for showing off her headdress (pictured) made with feather from 80 kingfishers . Peking opera singer Liu Guijuan wrote in her post on Weibo, China's equivalent of Twitter, that she had bought the rare headpiece more than a decade ago for 120,000 yuan (£10,775). 'It […]
summary_A: Opera singer Liu Guijuan faced backlash after posting pictures of a headdress made from the feathers of 80 kingfishers, purchased for 120,000 yuan (£10,775). Conservationists and web users criticized her for disregarding animal welfare, with some calling for her to step down. While some defended her, citing industry rules and artistic tradition, others suggested using fake feathers instead. Liu initially defended her actions but later removed the post; two of China's 11 kingfisher species are protected, and police in Guangdong recently seized 60,000 dead kingfishers.
summary_B: Peking opera singer Liu Guijuan posted pictures of her headdress on Weibo. It was made from the feathers of no less than 80 kingfishers. She said she bought the rare headpiece more than a decade ago for 120,000 yuan (£10,775) Two of the 11 types of kingfisher in China are protected species.

In not-so-subtle posts on the social networking site, the two carriers reignited their feud by posting tweets concerning their operation at Dublin Airport. Ryanair, run by Michael O'Leary, shared a photo of two of its staff by an advertising banner in Terminal 2, along with the words: 'Low Fares have come to @DublinAirport T2 at last. 'Fly from T1 for the lowest fares made simple.' Ryanair took to Twitter for a cheeky promotional photo in Terminal 2 in Dublin - where Aer Lingus fly out from . In response to Ryanair's post, Aer Lingus had a dig at where Ryanair fly their passengers out too . Ryanair […]
summary_A: Ryanair and Aer Lingus engage in light-hearted banter on Twitter. Ryanair posts photo of staff in Terminal 2 at Dublin Airport. Aer LingUS responds by saying 'Fly from T2 at @DublinAirport to central locations across Europe. T1 gets you nearly there, we get you really there'
summary_B: Ryanair and Aer Lingus engaged in another Twitter feud, exchanging jabs about their operations at Dublin Airport. Ryanair posted a promotional photo in Terminal 2, where Aer Lingus operates, prompting Aer Lingus to respond with a dig at Ryanair's use of smaller, less central airports. This follows a previous Twitter spat in January over Ryanair using an Aer Lingus plane in its promotional material. The rivalry occurs as the UK Court of Appeal prepares to rule on Ryanair's stake in Aer Lingus, which may force Ryanair to reduce its ownership due to competition regulations.

Alaba, out for three months earlier this season after a partial ligament tear in his right knee, was injured while playing for Austria in their 1-1 draw against Bosnia on Tuesday. 'I am bitterly disappointed,' the 22-year-old told the club's website. 'But I have a big aim and that is to be there at the season finale.' David Alaba is tackled by Emir Spahic's tackle during Austria's 1-1 draw against Bosnia-Herzegovina . summary_A: David Alaba was injured while playing for Austria in their 1-1 draw against Bosnia-Herzegovina on Tuesday. The 22-year-old is set to start rehabilitation work in about a month. Bayern Munich face Porto in the Champions League quarter-finals later this month.
summary_B: Bayern Munich's left-back David Alaba will miss the season's closing stages due to a torn knee ligament, sidelining him for around seven weeks. The injury occurred during Austria's 1-1 draw against Bosnia, marking his second significant knee injury this season. Alaba expressed disappointment but aims to return for the season finale. He had been instrumental in Bayern's pursuit of a treble, with the team currently leading the Bundesliga and advancing in the German Cup and Champions League.

article_excerpt: Washington (CNN)In 2011, al Qaeda took Warren Weinstein hostage. Then, about a year later, his family paid money to his captors, said a Pakistani source who was in regular contact with the kidnappers. It did not lead to the American aid worker's release, and he was inadvertently killed in an anti-terror strike in January, the White House announced Thursday. After the transfer of funds in 2012, the captors, who never referred to themselves as "al Qaeda," but instead as "Afghans," began demanding prisoners be released in exchange for Weinstein, most prominently Dr. Aafia Siddiqui of Pakistan, the source said. She has been described as the "poster girl" for Islamic jihad and is serving an 86-year sentence in the United States. […]
summary_A: Warren Weinstein's family paid money to his captors, a Pakistani source says. It did not lead to the American aid worker's release, and he was inadvertently killed in an anti-terror strike. After the transfer of funds in 2012, the captors began demanding prisoners be released in exchange for Weinstein.
summary_B: Warren Weinstein, an American aid worker, was taken hostage by al Qaeda in 2011 and later killed in a U.S. anti-terror strike in January 2015. His family paid a ransom to his captors in 2012, but it did not secure his release, and the captors later demanded prisoner exchanges, including Dr. Aafia Siddiqui. The captors, who identified as "Afghans," maintained regular contact with a Pakistani source, boasting of connections to other terror events and threatening Weinstein's life. Despite efforts by Weinstein's family and Maryland lawmakers to secure his release, including meetings with U.S. and Pakistani officials, he was inadvertently killed in a drone strike, leading to emotional reactions from those involved in his case.

summary_A: World No. 1 Novak Djokovic apologized to a ball boy he startled during a heated outburst at his support team in the Miami Open final against Andy Murray. Djokovic, frustrated after losing the second set, snatched a towel from the ball boy, prompting a code violation from the umpire. In a Facebook video, Djokovic expressed regret, emphasizing no intent to harm or scare the boy and extending his apology to the boy's parents. Despite the incident, Djokovic rallied to win the match 7-6, 4-6, 6-0, claiming his fifth Miami Open title.
summary_B: Novak Djokovic lost his cool at the end of the second set of the Miami Open final against Andy Murray. The world No 1 grabbed a towel from the ball boy who seemed startled by the loud confrontation. The youngster was caught in the crossfire of a tirade at his support team during his win over Murray in Sunday's final. The Serbian issued an apology via Facebook.

Steven Sloan, joined by friends Michael Niccum and Eugene Dight were on an aluminium rowboat when the encounter occurred off the west coast of Anderson Island, Washington. Filming from the boat, Steven captured the orcas swimming from afar – two of them can be seen jumping from the water. At a safe distance: The group cheer in excitment as Steven captures two orcas swimming and jumping from the water . summary_A: Steven Sloan, joined by friends Michael Niccum and Eugene Dight were on an aluminium rowboat when the encounter occurred off the west coast of Anderson Island, Washington. The group believe that the sound of the rope being pulled along the side of the boat is what attracted the orcas.
summary_B: Three friends, Steven Sloan, Michael Niccum, and Eugene Dight, encountered a pod of baby killer whales while crabbing off Anderson Island, Washington. Initially excited, they filmed the orcas swimming and jumping from a distance, but grew nervous as the whales approached their aluminum rowboat. Believing the sound of a rope being pulled attracted the orcas, the group panicked as one whale emerged close to the boat, with one member shouting, "We need to get out of here." The whales circled the boat, prompting nervous laughter and pleas from the group, who eventually rowed back to shore. Steven later shared the video, inviting viewers to laugh at their reaction and enjoy the orcas.

article_excerpt: Breakthrough?: Early tests carried out on cancer cells (like the one pictured) have shown survival rates in mice were boosted by more than 50 per cent . A new technique that effectively gives a personal treatment for cancer has been found by scientists. It harnesses the power of the body’s immune system and targets it at tumours. Early experiments have demonstrated that the new method could revolutionise cancer care. Scientists have found a system of priming the body’s immune system to recognise, attack and kill off cancerous cells in lung, skin and bowel tumours. The team which carried out the research found that early trials ‘profoundly retarded’ tumour growth in mice. Survival rates were boosted by more than 50 per […]
summary_A: New technique harnesses the power of the body’s immune system and targets it at tumours. Early experiments have demonstrated that the new method could revolutionise cancer care. Scientists are now recruiting patients with skin cancer for the first clinical trial on humans. British experts said it is the most promising sign yet that ‘personal’ treatments may be effective in treating a wide range of cancers.
summary_B: Scientists have developed a new cancer treatment technique that harnesses the body's immune system to target and kill cancerous cells in lung, skin, and bowel tumors. Early experiments on mice showed a 50% increase in survival rates, with the treatment "profoundly retarding" tumor growth. The method involves creating personalized vaccines based on an individual's tumor genetic makeup, boosting the immune system's T-cells to detect and destroy cancer cells. The first human clinical trial is set to begin with skin cancer patients, and experts believe this approach may provide a universal blueprint for targeting various human cancers.

article_excerpt: A hero pilot pulled his plane out of a terrifying North Sea nosedive with just seven seconds to spare. The plane began to plunge after it was struck by lightning, but autopilot ignored the pilot’s commands to climb and tried to crash the plane into the sea. The airliner pitched down, falling at 9,500ft a minute, and fell to just 1,100ft above the ocean before its commander wrestled back control just moments before it was about to crash into the icy water. The Loganair flight was just seconds from crashing into the north sea before its commander saved the day . The 42-year-old pilot put out a Mayday emergency signal before regaining control and saving his 30 passengers and three […]
summary_A: Loganair flight from Aberdeen to Shetland was struck by lightning. autopilot ignored pilot's commands to climb and tried to crash the plane into the sea. Pilot wrestled back control just moments before it was about to crash into the icy water. The aircraft landed safely in Aberdeen with only minor damage and no injuries.
summary_B: A Loganair flight from Aberdeen to Shetland narrowly avoided crashing into the North Sea after being struck by lightning, which caused the autopilot to malfunction and send the plane into a nosedive. The pilot regained control just 1,100ft above the ocean, saving 30 passengers and three crew members. The incident occurred on December 15 during severe weather conditions, and the plane landed safely in Aberdeen with minor damage. An investigation by the AAIB found no technical faults with the aircraft, attributing the dive to the autopilot system countering the pilot's actions, and pilot training now includes simulations of the event.

The clip shows the very moment the helmet camera becomes detached and makes its dizzying descent back to earth. After what begins as a routine skydive - with two of the jumpers linking hands in mid-air as two companions circle them - the camera slips from helmet and makes its stomach-churning plunge to the ground. It spins quickly to the ground for a minute and a half before crashing into a field. Remarkably, the camera remains intact despite falling from the great height. The video was taken of a routine skydive in Everöd, Sweden and […]
summary_A: The video was taken of a routine skydive in Everöd, Sweden and recorded on the helmet of one of the divers. The camera slips from helmet and makes its stomach-churning plunge to the ground. Remarkably, the camera remains intact despite falling from the great height.
summary_B: A GoPro camera detached from a skydiver's helmet at 10,000 feet during a routine skydive in Everöd, Sweden, capturing its dizzying freefall to the ground. The camera spun uncontrollably for one and a half minutes before crashing into a field in Gringelstad, remarkably remaining intact. The footage, believed to be four years old, was found by Kristoffer Örstadius's father, who uploaded it to YouTube, leading to the owner's identification. The video has since amassed over 250,000 views, showcasing the camera's dramatic descent and survival.

The baby elephant dawdles, picks something up with its trunk, and disrupts the tail-to-trunk connection between the last two elephants. But one young elephant decided to go it alone, when it walked alongside its herd and even broke their chain. Captured at Whipsnade Zoo, the video shows keepers assisting six elephants along a path.

summary_A: Cody got stuck in the bog in Belvedere, south-east London. Fire crews worked for an hour and a half to free the distressed animal. The horse was covered head to hoof in mud after being dragged to safety. He has been taken back to the stables to be seen by a vet.
summary_B: Cody, a horse, got stuck in a muddy bog in Belvedere, south-east London, on Friday afternoon. summary_A: The Research Vessel Flip (RV Flip), a 355-foot scientific platform, has been used by the US Office for Naval Research for over 50 years. It lacks an engine and is towed to its destination, where it flips 90 degrees, leaving only 50 feet above the surface, providing exceptional stability for research. The vessel uses ballast tanks to shift its center of gravity, completing the flip in 20 minutes. It accommodates five crew and eleven researchers for up to 30 days, conducting studies in underwater acoustics, oceanography, meteorology, and marine mammal observation. Launched in 1962, it was initially vital for submarine development during the Cold War and has since been used for marine life and weather research.
summary_B: Vessel has been used by the US Office for Naval Research for more than 50 years. It is used to measure underwater acoustics as well as water temperature. It can be also used for oceanography, meteorology and marine mammal observation. The vessel can accommodate five crew and up to eleven researchers for up to 30 days.

summary_A: Fascinating video shows twisting groups of magnetic fields writhing around. They are essentially twisted bundles of magnetic field that extend out of and back into the surface across hundreds of kilometres. As common structures in the solar corona, they are thought to be the main cause of several types of solar weather - including solar flares and CMEs.
summary_B: Researchers from the New Jersey Institute of Technology, led by Dr. Haimin Wang, have captured the first high-resolution footage of solar flux ropes, revealing their twisting magnetic fields and formation process. The video shows an S-shaped bundle of magnetic fields evolving into a multi-stranded flux rope, accompanied by a solar flare. These structures, common in the solar corona, are believed to cause solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), impacting space weather and potentially damaging satellites, airlines, and electricity grids. The study, published in *Nature Communications*, aims to enhance understanding of flux rope formation and their role in solar eruptions.

summary_B: Scientists from the University of East Anglia warn that the growing demand for rubber, primarily driven by the tyre industry, is causing significant deforestation, with up to 21 million acres of jungle expected to be cleared for rubber plantations by 2024.
